transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is this constant tightness. My neck and shoulders, and even my jaw, they’re just clenched most of the time now. It’s like I’m bracing myself for bad news, even when nothing is happening—just sitting at my desk or trying to watch television in the evening.

I mean, I’m a teacher, so sitting at a desk isn’t exactly unusual, and you’d think after all these years I’d be used to it, but this feels different. I’ll notice my shoulders are up around my ears for no reason, and I have to sort of remind myself to relax. It’s been wearing me down.
Have you been having sudden surges of intense fear or discomfort that come on abruptly?

I don’t think so… not in that sudden, out-of-nowhere way, if that’s what you mean. I mean, I do get worked up, but it’s more like it builds and lingers rather than hitting me like a lightning bolt.

Though, funny enough, when the fire alarm goes off at school during drills, I still jump like everyone else—probably more than the students, which they find hilarious. But that’s not really what you’re asking, is it? So… no, I haven’t noticed sudden surges like that.
Did this start after a particular stressful event or change in your life?

Yes… I think it did, actually. It’s been about seven months now, if I’m counting right. We had a pipe burst at the house, and then the remodeling just turned everything upside down.

I remember thinking at first, “Well, it’s just a house repair, people deal with worse,” and the contractor kept saying it would only be a few weeks—though you know how that goes, one wall opens up and suddenly there’s another problem behind it. My wife joked we should just move into the hardware store. But yes, that’s when it really seemed to start, when the house was in chaos.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not just the house anymore, although that’s where my mind goes first—like, did the contractors miss something behind a wall, is there another leak waiting to show up, that sort of thing.

But then it jumps. I’ll be grading papers and suddenly I’m thinking my lesson plans aren’t as solid as they used to be, or the robotics club kids are falling behind because I’m not organized enough. And then somehow that turns into worrying I’m letting my wife down, or the family, because I should be able to keep everything under control.

It’s like my brain can’t stay on one worry. It just keeps looking for the next thing.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I have days where I feel worn down or discouraged, sure—who wouldn’t, with everything feeling like it’s piled up?

But “down” as in… I don’t know, that word makes me think of not wanting to get out of bed or losing interest in everything. I still do my classes, still show up. Although last week I did stand in front of the copier for five minutes waiting for copies I hadn’t actually pressed start on, which the office secretary found funnier than I did.

So… I guess I’ve felt stressed and kind of heavy at times, but I’m not sure I’d say depressed.
Have you been feeling this worried on most days for at least six months?

Yes… most days, I’d say. It’s been about seven months since that pipe burst and the remodeling turned the house upside down.

At first I thought it was just normal stress, you know, dust everywhere, plastic sheets in the hall, never being able to find a coffee mug because everything was packed in the wrong box… but it hasn’t really let up. So yes, at least six months.
When you start worrying, do you find it hard to stop or control the worry?

Yes. That’s probably the worst part, honestly. I can tell myself, “Stop it, pay attention to the class in front of you,” and I’ll even be writing something on the board, but then one little thing gets in.

Like if I remember there’s a late invoice, or I notice a student hasn’t turned something in, suddenly it’s not just that one thing. It becomes, “What if this leads to that, and then what if I missed something else?” It just starts branching out.

And I know it’s not useful. I know sitting there running through it doesn’t fix the invoice or help the student, but it’s like I can’t get my mind to put it down. Even when I try to redirect myself, it circles back.
Has your anxiety continued even as the house repairs have settled down?

Yes… it has, unfortunately. I kept thinking once the contractors were gone and the house wasn’t in pieces anymore, my brain would quiet down.

But now it just sort of hops tracks. I’ll start wondering if they missed something behind a wall, and then suddenly I’m thinking my lesson plans are getting sloppy, or the robotics kids are falling behind—one of them asked me about a sensor last week and I gave him this completely muddled answer, though to be fair those little parts all look the same after a while.

And then it turns into whether I’m letting my wife down, or the family, because I’m not keeping everything under control the way I’m supposed to. So yes, the house is better, but the worrying didn’t really pack up and leave with the contractors.
